memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Anyone with such a defiling disease must wear torn clothes, let their hair be unkempt, cover the lower part of their face and cry out, 'Unclean! Unclean!' As long as they have the disease they remain unclean. They must live alone; they must live outside the camp." - Lev 13:45-46 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
These are among the saddest verses in the Bible. Torn clothes. Unkempt hair. A covered face. And a voice calling out the worst thing you could say about yourself, over and over, as a warning to everyone approaching.

They must live alone. Outside the camp — away from family, away from worship, away from every ordinary human comfort.

We should not rush past this. God is showing His people something terrible and true: that corruption separates. Sin does this. It isolates us from God and from each other. Isaiah put it plainly — your iniquities have separated you from your God (Isa 59:2).

Now hold that picture, and watch what happens centuries later. A man with this very condition comes to Jesus and kneels. He should not even be there; he should be calling out a warning. And Jesus, filled with compassion, reached out his hand and touched the man (Mark 1:41).

Touched him. The untouchable one.

And then the greater wonder still. Hebrews tells us that Jesus suffered outside the city gate (Heb 13:12) — He went to the place of the excluded. The Clean One took the position of the unclean, so that those living outside the camp could be brought home.

Whatever has made you feel unfit to come near, He has already come out to where you are.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Have you ever felt like the person outside the camp?
2. What have you believed makes you unfit to come near to God?
3. Who around you is living "outside the camp" that you could reach towards?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord Jesus, thank You that You went outside the camp for me and touched what everyone else avoided. Bring me home, and make me someone who reaches towards the excluded. Amen.
